I hold out the note. "This is also from me, for a dyer's daughter named Wren, twelve, who sweeps the chapel there and wants to learn the work. Maud Marrow vouches for her, and her parents have agreed to a month's trial. Will you read it, and will you see Tobin today?"

input.add_to_description: Day 6 morning: met Brannoc. Heavy woman of sixty with smith's forearms, loud and blunt, baking when he arrived. She knew Edda Thorne by reputation. She agreed to see Tobin that day, and took Brannoc's note about Wren.

entries.text:
Aldith doesn't stop kneading until you've finished. Then she wipes her hands on her apron, takes the note between a floury finger and thumb, and reads it standing, with her lips moving. She reads it twice.

"Edda Thorne's boy," she says. "She set a collarbone of mine forty years back, when I was young and thought bones were simple. Hmph. She's dead, then." It isn't a question, and she doesn't wait for you to answer. She folds the note small and tucks it into her bodice. "Gods keep her. I'm sorry. You'll have your tea first."

Then she starts on your matters, one at a time. "The boy. A crushed ankle, a day old, and not set? Ansel knows better than to leave it. Send him on his litter and I'll have him on this table by the hour. I'll want the swelling down a bit, so he'll sit with his foot up and be bored. Crushed's not the worst. Crushed and clean, I can do. It's the ones that heal wrong that make me cuss."

At Perrin's hip she grunts. "A month crooked? Aye. I can break and reset it, but it's a bad business and a long one. Weeks on his back, and an old man's bones don't love it. He'll have to want it himself. I don't go hunting men who'd rather limp. Tell him to come to me, or send word, and I'll see him. Maud's blankets keep my feet warm. I'll not turn her friend's friend away."

On Wren she is slower. She turns the matter over, looking not at you but at the fire. "Twelve. Sweeping a dead priest's chapel because no one else would. That's a girl who stays, I'd wager." She sniffs. "A month's trial, parents' leave, Maud to bring her. Good. I won't have children running off from their mothers. I've had three prentices and kept two, and I'm not too proud to take a third if she's got a stomach and doesn't faint at the sight of a bone. Tell her to bring a clean apron and a stout heart, and not to be late."

She thumps a mug of tea down in front of you, strong and bitter. "Now sit. Drink. You've the look of a man who's not slept right since he left home."

It's twenty to seven. Tobin is a few streets away waiting for his litter. Your errands here are nearly all done. You are 100 XP short of the next rung, the Drowned Stair is sealed, and the valley road runs on south past the town.

input.add_to_description: Day 6 morning: Met Brannoc, read his note about Wren, agreed to see Tobin today. Will not decide on Wren without seeing the girl; wants her sent with Maud when the weather holds. Says Perrin's hip needs breaking and resetting, to be done only in her house, and only if Perrin comes himself.

entries.text:
Mother Aldith doesn't stop kneading. She holds out one floury hand, takes the note between two fingers and reads it with her lips pressed thin. She reads it twice.

"Edda Thorne's boy," she says. "I met your Edda once, forty years back, at a bad birthing. She didn't say much. She didn't need to." She sniffs. "Maud Marrow vouches for the girl, does she? That woman talks the ears off a mill-wheel, but she's never once lied to me. A month's trial, with her parents' say-so. That's more sense than most come with."

She wipes her hands on her apron and drops the note on the table. "I'll not promise the girl a place. I'll see her hands and hear her talk, and I'll know in a morning. Have her sent down with Maud when the weather holds. If she faints at blood, she goes home. If she asks me why every time I tell her to do something, she'll do."

The crushed ankle gets a harder look. "Ansel's boy? Yes. Have him carried here by noon, and I'll set it while he's too sore to fight me. It's a fresh break, not an old one, and it will mend straight if it's done right." Then she turns on the hip. "Your dyer. A hip that's healed wrong must be broken again and reset, and it's ugly work. I won't do it on a road or in a dye-shed. He comes to me himself, on his own two feet, and he makes up his own mind. A man who's dragged here fights the bone, and the bone wins. Tell him that. Tell him it hurts, and that he'll walk straight after. Both are true."

She jerks her chin at the bench. "Sit. Eat something before you go preaching at anyone else. You look like you slept in a barn."

It's a little before twenty to seven on Day 6. You've two 1st-level slots and Channel Divinity, and 100 XP to go to level 3. Tobin's litter will be at the door by noon, and the road to the next place without a healer lies open.

input.add_to_description: Day 6 ~6:30 AM: Met Brannoc. Read his note, agrees to a month's trial for Wren if Maud brings her. Will set Tobin's ankle at noon Day 6 and wants Brannoc present to ease the boy's pain. Will reset Perrin's hip only if he comes to Stonebridge (about three weeks laid up), charging what he can pay.

entries.text:
Mother Aldith will see Tobin at noon today. She wants you at his side when she sets the ankle, to ease his pain. Both tool calls (the notebook entry and the clock) did go through, but I made them after I'd written the scene, so they came late. The clock now reads 6:30 AM.

The scene stands as written. Aldith also said she won't reset Perrin's hip unless he comes to Stonebridge, and he'd be laid up about three weeks. She'll take Wren on a month's trial if Maud brings her.

You have a few hours before noon. You have two 1st-level slots and Channel Divinity ready.

What does Brannoc do?

Aldith doesn't stop kneading. She holds out a floury elbow for the note, and you lay it on her forearm. She reads it with her lips moving, then reads it again, slowly.

"Edda's boy. She wrote to me twice in forty years, and both times it was to tell me I was wrong." She snorts, and it might be a laugh. "Maud Marrow's name on a girl, is it? Maud weaves my winter blankets and she's never once let me forget the price. Twelve is old enough to learn, and young enough to be spoiled by a bad teacher. I'm a bad teacher. Tell her parents that, so nobody weeps later."

She slaps the dough into a pan and wipes her hands on her apron. "A month's trial is sense. I'll take her if she doesn't faint at the sight of bone. Have Maud bring her down when the weather holds, and I'll see what she's made of."

Then she looks at you properly. "The boy. Crushed ankle, you say. How long, and was it bruised black or only swollen? Send him over on Ansel's litter. I'll set it at noon, while I've a clear table. It'll hurt him, and he'll scream. If you've a prayer that eases a child's pain and steadies his heart when I pull, you'll stand by and say it. I'll not turn down a cleric's hands."

On the hip, her face goes flat. "A month healed crooked, and a dyer too proud to see anyone. I can't go to him. A bone that's knit wrong has to be broken again and reset, and I won't do it in a dye-shed, on a man who's not asked. He'd have to come here. Three weeks laid up, if he's lucky, and he'll hate me for it. Tell him that straight. If he comes, I'll do it for Maud's sake and charge him only what he can pay."

It's about half past six. The hospice is close, Tobin needs to eat before the litter, and you have two 1st-level slots and Channel Divinity ready. You also have a few hours before noon.

line:
"Good morning, Mother Aldith. I'm Brannoc Ashdown, Edda Thorne's foster-son, and I've come with two matters. A boy named Tobin has a crushed ankle at Brother Ansel's hospice, and a dyer in Greywater, Perrin Gale, has a hip that healed crooked after a fall from a rack."

I hold out the note. "This is also from me, for a dyer's daughter named Wren, twelve, who sweeps the chapel there and wants to learn the work. Maud Marrow vouches for her, and her parents have agreed to a month's trial. Will you read it, and will you see Tobin today?"

entries.text:
Aldith wipes one hand on her apron and takes the note with two floury fingers. She reads it standing, lips moving, and then reads it again. "Edda Thorne's lad," she says. "She set a collarbone for me once, forty years back, and told me I held a hammer like a woman who'd never been hit. She was right." She tucks the note into her apron.

She goes through your matters in order, the way a person does who counts bones for a living.

"The boy first. A crush, you say? Then it's today, and not by a litter that jolts him over the cobbles. I'll walk to the hospice myself when this dough is in. Bone doesn't wait, and nor does a child's fear." She jerks her chin at you. "You'll hold him. Children bite and kick me, but they listen to a man in a mail shirt humming."

On Perrin's hip, her face closes up. "A month healed crooked is a hard one. I would have to see it, and I won't promise he'll thank me. Rebreaking a hip is no kindness, and a proud old man will curse me all the way through it. Tell him to come when the roads are dry, and bring someone to carry him home. Tell him I'll look first, and I'll tell him straight if I won't do it."

Then she pauses over the note, and for the first time she looks at you instead of the dough. "Maud Marrow's wool is on my bed, and I owe her more than a blanket's worth. A dyer's girl who wants to learn and has parents who said yes, which is rarer than you'd think. A month's trial, is it? I take that kindly. Two of my three stayed. The third was a fool, and I don't miss him. Send her down with Maud when the weather holds, and I'll see what she's made of. I'll tell you now that I'll work her until she cries, and then I'll work her more."

She slaps the dough into a pan and puts it by the hearth. "Well? Are you wanting breakfast, or just standing there? I've an hour before I can leave this house."

input.add_to_description: Day 14 ~4:45 PM scouting (Brannoc natural 20 Perception): Jory's skiff is still tied at the south tip, dry-hulled, one eel-spear lying in it. A trail of burned-down candle stubs leads from the shore along the mound's flank to the west door; the last stub, set on the sill, was still soft with wax (a day old at most), so Jory was alive recently. The door's lintel carries a worn carving of a spiral around a lamp, the same mark as on the Wayfarers' Lamp, and a stone niche beside it for a lamp, now empty and dark. The mounds of the Sleepers' Chain each had a keeper's lamp, and the reeds were an old cover over the barrow's sealing. Cutting them and letting the lamp lapse woke the sleeper. The Wick-fires did not stir toward the skiff. Brannoc returned to Reedholm by ~5:25 PM.

entries.text:
You take the rope, the hooded lantern and a few flasks, and settle in the skiff's bow while Wick poles and Gorm watches the reeds. The channels wind through the fen, black and still, and you speak only in whispers. The mist is thin, and your own breath smokes. The Wick-fires hang over the west side, steady and pale, and they do not stir as you come in. You keep your word. You turn at the south tip, and no one lands.

Perception (20, a natural 20): you see far more than you hoped.

Jory's skiff is there, tied to a stake at the south tip, its hull dry and one eel-spear lying in the bottom. From it a line of burned-down candle stubs runs along the mound's flank, one every few paces, like a boy who knew he'd need to find his way back. They lead to the west door. The last stub sits on the sill, and the wax is still soft. He was alive within the day. The lintel above the door carries a worn carving, a spiral wound round a lamp. It is the same mark you saw on the stones of the Wayfarers' Lamp. Beside the door is a stone niche, made for a lamp, and it is empty and dark.

It comes together in your mind as Wick poles you away. Each mound in the Sleepers' Chain had a keeper's lamp, and the reeds were an old cover laid over the barrow. The reed-cutters stripped that cover, and no lamp has burned in the niche for years. Whatever sleeps there has woken. The lights did not stir toward the skiff, and you think they follow warmth and flame more than they chase prey.

You are back at the staithe by twenty-five past five, with the dusk coming down. Ode meets you there, and you tell her about the skiff, the candles, and the soft wax. Her face does not change, but her hand tightens on the pole-hook.

You have four 1st-level slots, no 2nd-level slots, and Channel Divinity. You have thirty-seven flasks, a rope, two lanterns, and ten candles. Night falls now. Jory has been alive on the Isle for at least a day, perhaps five, and the lamp-niche stands cold at the west door.
